questions.question: Given `public class Dog { public string Name; public Dog(string name) { Name = name; } }`, which line is valid?
questions.explanation: Once you write any constructor, the free parameterless one disappears — `new Dog()` no longer works. You must supply the required argument: `new Dog("Rex")`.

questions.question: What does `this` refer to inside an instance method?
options: The class itself, not any particular object
The object the method was called on
questions.explanation: `this` is a reference to the specific object the method is currently running on — e.g. inside `rex.Bark()`, `this` is `rex`.

questions.question: Two `BankAccount` objects created with the same starting balance are `==` to each other.
questions.explanation: Classes use reference equality by default (Module 1's memory lesson). Two separate objects are never `==`, even with identical field values, unless the class explicitly overrides equality (records do this automatically — plain classes don't).

questions.question: In `public Dog(string name) { this.Name = name; }`, what would happen if you wrote `Name = Name;` instead of `this.Name = name;`?
options: Same result — this.Name and Name are always interchangeable
The field Name would be set to itself (unchanged/default) — the parameter `name` would never be used
It would throw a runtime exception
questions.explanation: `Name` alone refers to the field (assuming no local shadowing), so `Name = Name;` just assigns the field to itself — the parameter `name` is silently ignored. This exact mistake is why `this.Name = name;` matters when field and parameter share a name (case-insensitively similar).
